\chapter{Reading — Words, Lines, and a First Scene}
\label{ch:la-prima-lectio}
\hlchaptermodality{58}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read familiar Latin words cold, follow whole lines by their endings, and hold a connected meeting scene without translating word by word.}

Forty-two familiar words gathered into one meeting scene, with macrons, cases, demonstratives, and verb endings carrying the information English spreads across more words.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[(reading)]{(reading) — six words, and length made visible}

\label{lesson:LA-C58-verba}



\begin{quote}
Every word below is old. The new work is meeting it first with your eyes.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
salvē avē valē grātiās ita nōn
\end{quote}

Read down once without stopping.

Again, and let each macron hold its vowel for the length you already know from hearing it.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a mark Romans did not need}]
The line over a vowel is a \textbf{macron}. Ancient Romans normally did not write one. This book does because vowel length can distinguish words and because a beginning reader deserves to see what a careful speaker says.

So the mark is not decoration and it is not an accent. In \textbf{salvē} and \textbf{valē}, it asks you to hold the final vowel. In \textbf{grātiās}, it does the same job twice.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the six words in order, once, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many words were new? (\textbf{None.})

What does a macron tell a reader? (\textbf{Hold that vowel long.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(reading)]{(reading) — six lines, and the person at the end}

\label{lesson:LA-C58-lineae}



\begin{quote}
The last lesson gave you isolated words. These are whole lines.

You have already said every one of them.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
Salvē! Quid agis? Valeō. Grātiās tibi agō. Mihi nōmen est Mārcus. Valē!
\end{quote}

Read down once without stopping.

Again, and this time watch the last letter of \textbf{agis}, \textbf{valeō} and \textbf{agō}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the person rides on the verb}]
Latin does not need to write \textbf{ego}, “I,” before \textbf{valeō} or \textbf{agō}. The \textbf{-ō} already says who acts. In \textbf{agis}, the \textbf{-s} points to “you.”

That makes a Latin line short without making it incomplete. A reader looks to the verb's right edge for a person English usually puts at the left.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the six lines in order, once, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does a Latin reader find the person when there is no written pronoun? (\textbf{On the verb ending.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(reading)]{(reading) — the first connected scene}

\label{lesson:LA-C58-prima-lectio}



\begin{quote}
Six words, then six lines. Now the lines become one meeting.

Forty-two words, and every one has already appeared in an earlier lesson.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
Salvē! Mihi nōmen est Mārcus. Quid tibi nōmen est? Mihi nōmen est Iūlia. Quid agis? Valeō, grātiās tibi agō. Et tū? Valeō. Haec est soror mea. Illa est māter mea. Haec aqua est. Ille pānis est. Ante merīdiem est. Post merīdiem, valē!
\end{quote}

Read the whole scene once without stopping. Let the endings tell you who acts, and let the cases keep each name and relationship in place.

Read it again. This time follow the three pointers: \textbf{haec}, \textbf{illa}, \textbf{ille}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Latin holds together without articles}]
English would keep supplying “the” and written pronouns. Latin does not. \textbf{Haec aqua est} needs no article; \textbf{valeō} needs no \textbf{ego}. Gender, case and verb ending carry the links instead.

That is why the scene can look spare while saying everything it needs. Reading Latin is not filling in missing English words. It is learning to trust the information Latin chose to write.

The final pair does the same work with time. \textbf{Ante} and \textbf{post} put the scene on opposite sides of \textbf{merīdiēs} without a longer explanation.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the scene aloud, once, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What holds the Latin scene together without articles and repeated pronouns? (\textbf{Gender, case, and verb endings.})
\end{tcolorbox}
